units.title: OP Stack chains with a non-ETH gas token
angles: Arithmetic and control flow. Read the interpreter this network runs at the release its endpoint reports, and any compiler, bytecode rewriting, caching or code analysis stage in front of it. Cover the 256 bit integer library and its pinned version, MULMOD, ADDMOD, DIV, SDIV, MOD, SMOD, SIGNEXTEND, SAR, SHL, SHR, BYTE, EXP, the comparisons, JUMP and JUMPI with the jump destination analysis, KECCAK256, MCOPY, memory expansion and CALLDATALOAD. Compare each with the Ethereum specification at the edges that OPCODES.md lists, and read the release notes and fix commits since the versions OPCODES.md records. Then rerun the scripts in research/network-risk/tools/opdiff (battery.py, targeted.py, pmdiff.py, pmdiff2.py, swaps.py, replay.py) for this unit's chain ids, write the outputs into your work directory, and add vectors for anything the reading makes suspicious. Report every result that differs from the specification, every release that changed these paths, how a wrong result would change the pool math in src/libraries (TickMath, BitMath, FullMath, SqrtPriceMath, SwapMath, TickBitmap) or the logic that depends on it, and which validators could run a different code path than the public endpoint.

Upcoming forks. Assume every network upgrade scheduled or proposed for the next six months ships. What changes for the PoolManager and for funds already inside it, and what could an ordinary account do the day after?

Do not install software. Python 3, rustc 1.97 with cargo, go 1.24, node and the system C and C++ compilers are present, and you may compile downloaded source inside your own work directory. Keep downloads and build output under a directory named build/ or dl/ inside your work directory. Do not download compiler toolchains or other binaries to run them; source archives are fine. Record every sampling seed, save every mismatch record in full, and bracket each batch of calls to a public endpoint with web3_clientVersion so the build that answered is known. Leads L-838, L-839 and L-829. Findings F-117 and F-136 record that the Go clients of several networks are built with Go releases that carry compiler faults: issue 81863 (https://github.com/golang/go/issues/81863, a store through a pointer chosen by a branch between two non-escaping stack locals is deleted; go1.26.0 to go1.26.10 and go1.27.0 to go1.27.3) and issue 82839 (https://github.com/golang/go/issues/82839, the prove pass carries a fact through a sign extension of an int8, int16 or int32 compared with a constant wider than the narrow type and takes a branch that cannot be taken; go1.26.6 to go1.26.10, go1.27.3, a variant from go1.24.13). bor v2.11.1, BNB Chain geth v1.8.2 and avalanchego 1.15.3 (libevm and coreth) are built with go1.26.10, Celo op-geth c7ed55b8 with go1.24.13, Nitro v3.13.0-rc.9 with go1.27.3, geth v1.17.9 with go1.27.2. Cycle 10 searched the 81863 shape only in Nitro's go-ethereum fork at 0e44603, and cycle 17 searched geth v1.17.9; nobody searched bor, BNB Chain geth, libevm, coreth or Celo op-geth, and nobody searched any client for the 82839 shape. Task 1: read both issue pages and their fix changes and state each triggering shape precisely, and settle from the Go release notes and the backport issues whether go1.26.10 holds the 81863 backport (#81865). Task 2: download the source of holiman/uint256 v1.3.2 and v1.2.4, bor v2.11.1, bsc v1.8.2, libevm and coreth at the versions avalanchego v1.15.3 pins, celo-org/op-geth at c7ed55b8 (or the nearest readable commit) and geth v1.17.9, and search core/vm, core/state, core/types hashing, the trie and rlp encoders on the execution path and the uint256 library systematically for both shapes. Write the search as a script over the Go syntax tree (go/ast and go/types with the installed go 1.24 are available) so the result is a list a reader can rerun, and report the count of candidate sites per package and each candidate with file and line. Task 3: for each candidate, say which opcode, copy offset, gas computation or state write it serves, and whether the PoolManager's bytecode can reach it with inputs an ordinary account controls (name the PoolManager function and the source line in src/). Use the installed toolchain's SSA dump (GOSSAFUNC) where it helps to show whether the faulty rewrite could apply; say plainly that the installed go 1.24 is not the affected compiler. Task 4: for every candidate on an opcode path, build vectors that would give a wrong word if the branch were mistaken or the store dropped and run them with eth_call and state overrides on Polygon, BNB Chain, Avalanche, Celo (pinned to the op-geth backend), Arbitrum One and Robinhood Chain. A candidate that an ordinary account can reach and that changes a PoolManager result is a finding with actor unprivileged; a candidate nobody can reach from the PoolManager is a cleared item with its reason.

Cycle 17 confirmed that the native code Monad v0.16.5 emits for the PoolManager depends on heap addresses: the block-exit writer in category/vm/compiler/ir/x86/emitter.cpp (about lines 1380 to 1540 at v0.16.5; a copy is in research/network-risk/cycles/016/theme-monad-harness-exact.work/dl/monad-0.16.5) iterates a container keyed by pointers, so two validators can run different machine code for the same contract. Results were equal on four heap layouts by test; nobody argued from the source that every order gives the same final stack. v0.16.7 removed the dependence. Task 1: read the writer and the functions it calls and prove or refute order independence. Answer three questions with line numbers: does the spill step before the dependency loop remove every dependency cycle; is a dependency that is skipped at the AVX register check ever read later from a register that an earlier write in the loop reassigned; can an element whose stack offset lies below min_delta be left with a nonzero dependency count. Task 2: turn the argument into a test. Using the harness in research/network-risk/cycles/016/theme-monad-harness-exact.work and research/network-risk/cycles/017/theme-monad-exact-sites.work (build.sh, link.sh, src/run.sh), force the iteration order of the writer (for example by a patched comparator or by sorting the container in every permutation for blocks with up to 6 live elements and in at least 200 seeded shuffles for larger ones) and run every basic block of the deployed PoolManager build on chain 143, comparing the stack, memory, storage, transient storage, gas and status with the interpreter after each block exit. Report the number of blocks, the largest dependency set seen and any order that gives a different result. Task 3: settle which release mainnet validators run. Look for a version in block headers or extra data, in monad-bft vote or proposal messages, in the validator set RPC, in public validator dashboards and in release announcements of category-labs, and compare the client string of each public endpoint (eth RPC web3_clientVersion on at least five endpoints). Task 4: if any order gives a different result, find the PoolManager function, the source line in src/ and the input an ordinary account would send to reach that block, and say whether a validator split or a wrong balance follows. That is a finding with actor unprivileged on chain 143.

Leads L-842, L-845, L-464 and L-830. PoolManager.sync (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288) needs no unlock and writes the synced currency and reserves to transient storage; settle (src/PoolManager.sol:349-364) credits the balance rise since sync to its caller. Everything rests on transient storage being empty at the start of every transaction. On HyperEVM cycle 17 tested that directly: a call trace of all 2,782 PoolManager transactions found none that ended with an ERC-20 still synced, so no later settle could meet a leaked sync (research/network-risk/cycles/017/hyperevm.work/l185.py). MegaETH's sequencer is closed and parallel and Monad executes optimistically in parallel; nobody has run the same census there. Task 1: on MegaETH (chain 4326, PoolManager 0xacb7e78fa05d562e0a5d3089ec896d57d057d38e, about 51,000 PoolManager transactions per cycle 15; the transaction lists of earlier cycles are under research/network-risk/cycles/015 and cycles/016/theme-megaeth-validator-build.work) and on Monad (chain 143), find every transaction that calls sync with a nonzero currency and ends, successfully, without a settle that clears it. For each, look at every later transaction of the same block that calls settle, settleFor or take on the PoolManager and decide from its trace or its logs and balance changes whether it was credited with a balance it did not pay in that transaction. Say how you found the transactions (trace method, log scan, receipts) and how complete the census is. Task 2: the same census for one OP Stack network with flashblocks (Base or Unichain) and for BNB Chain, sampled over at least 20,000 PoolManager transactions each, as a control. Task 3, silent log gaps: cycle 17 found that bsc-rpc.publicnode.com answers eth_getLogs with an empty list and no error for PoolManager logs of blocks 135,480,000 to 135,489,999 while the receipts of those blocks hold such logs. For the publicnode, pocket and official endpoints that earlier log censuses used on Base, Polygon, Avalanche, Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, OP Mainnet and BNB Chain, pick ten windows of 2,000 blocks spread from deployment to head and compare the eth_getLogs count of PoolManager Swap and ModifyLiquidity logs with the count from the receipts of 20 sampled blocks per window. List every endpoint that returns fewer logs than the receipts hold, and name which earlier results in research/network-risk/OPCODES.md rested on it. Task 4: enumerate the zero-value failed PoolManager calls on MegaETH before block 31,861,608 if a trace or receipt method allows it. A transaction credited from another transaction's sync is a finding with actor unprivileged; say whose money moved.

HyperEVM's validator is closed, so its arithmetic is tested through what it produced: 2.26 million Uniswap v3 style swaps on chain 999, which use the same FullMath, SqrtPriceMath and TickMath formulas as src/libraries. research/network-risk/cycles/017/hyperevm.work/v3check_rest.py reruns each swap from the pool state at the parent block and requires price, tick, liquidity and both amounts to equal the log to the unit (inputs under research/network-risk/cycles/015/theme-closed-producers-2.work/raw). Cycle 17 ran 7,000 of 20,000 sampled groups (--only 'm512?' --seed 3 --limit 20000 --threads 8) and counted 7 swaps that did not reproduce, but saved neither the records nor examined them. An own check after the cycle reran the same 7,000 groups with every mismatch saved: read research/network-risk/cycles/017/own-check.work (v3check_own.py, out/stageB-own.log, out/stageB-own.json.mismatch.jsonl, and NOTES.md if present) first and start from its result. Task 1: for every saved mismatch, explain it or show that it cannot be explained. Fetch all logs of the pool in that block and the block before, including topics the collector does not read (the 0xd78218c0 Mint variant with liquidity in data word 2 and ticks in topics 2 and 3 explained all four mismatches of cycle 15), check the pool's factory and bytecode for a fork that changes the swap step (a dynamic or protocol fee, a different tick spacing rule, a rebasing or fee-on-transfer token), and rerun the swap step by step, printing for the first step that differs the inputs and outputs of each mulDiv, mulDivRoundingUp, getNextSqrtPriceFromInput or Output and getAmount0Delta or getAmount1Delta call. A swap whose logged values differ from the formulas of src/libraries/FullMath.sol:14-116 and src/libraries/SqrtPriceMath.sol on equal inputs, with no difference in the pool's own code to explain it, is a finding with actor unprivileged on chain 999: the validator would compute v4 swaps differently from the source too. Task 2: teach the collector the Mint variant and any other event Task 1 turns up, then run stage B on all the groups that no cycle has run (about 39,500 of the 'm512?' groups plus the remaining 13,000 of the sample), with the seed recorded and every mismatch saved, and apply Task 1 to each new mismatch. Report counts: swaps reproduced, calls on the 512 bit branch of mulDiv, swaps with several steps, mismatches explained by cause, mismatches left. Task 3: plant the three faults the script supports (--plant mulmod, fallback, tick) on a sample of 2,000 groups each and report how many swaps each plant breaks, so the reader knows the comparison can fail. Read-only eth_call and eth_getLogs on https://rpc.purroofgroup.com and https://rpc.hyperliquid.xyz/evm only.
